prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength give frequency standards with fractional uncertainty near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My final position is a single-part prize for B049, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. I have not changed the configuration since round 1, but the exchange sharpened what the citation must say. The discovery content is the magic-wavelength scheme: a trapping wavelength at which the light shift cancels for both clock levels, so thousands of neutral atoms are held Doppler- and recoil-free without perturbing the line. That removes the old trade-off between atom number and systematic control, which neither the comb (2005) nor ion control (2012) addressed. The evidence is the kind I trust as an experimentalist: a measured number, fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, reproduced at several independent laboratories and confirmed in remote clock comparisons, with the systematics budget (blackbody, lattice, collisional shifts) understood in quantitative detail. Six of eight members now carry it in their preferred configuration, and the support comes from members with different tastes and different fields, which I weigh as corroboration of the scientific case and not as a replacement for it. The two-name credit is compact: Katori for the proposal and first realization, Ye for driving the platform to the performance frontier and showing that many-body and density effects can be controlled. I would keep the citation on the concept and its realization, and not enumerate applications.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still the one Olsson states most sharply: if the discovery is the invention and first realization, Katori alone may be the cleaner attribution, and Ye's role is partly execution at record performance. Second, the chair's question whether this is discovery-class or instrument-class is open: Danielsson is right that, so far, constants tests have given null results and geodesy at scale is still a promise. A measured departure, such as an unexpected drift or a clock-comparison anomaly, would settle the matter in favour of discovery, and none has appeared. Third, the boundary against 2005 and 2012 has to be explained in public, and Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Lisdat and Ludlow stay outside the two names. I accept all three as real residual weaknesses, not as arguments that outweigh the reproducibility evidence.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the prize would still stand if only Katori were credited, and says Ye's contribution may be a better-executed second wave rather than part of the original invention.
responses.response: I think the prize would stand on Katori alone, and the committee should say so openly, but I would still credit Ye. My reasoning is experimental. A scheme proposed for neutral atoms in a lattice is only established when someone shows that the magic-wavelength condition survives real atoms: that lattice-induced and density-dependent shifts can be pushed to the 1e-18 level and that the result is not an artefact of one apparatus. That demonstration, and the subsequent understanding of collisional and many-body effects, is what turned a proposal into a clock that other laboratories could copy and compare, and I treat it as part of the realization and not as a lifetime award. Your own criterion, the original experiment and not merely the better later one, is met by the pair if the citation is framed around invention and realization. I would support wording that keeps the performance milestone inside the realization clause, and I would not support wording that rewards precision records as such. If the committee cannot accept that reading, B049 falls back to a single name more naturally than it becomes a different prize, and I would then want to hear the committee's view on whether one name is acceptable.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B049 eighth because the discovery content is so far a null result on constants and a promise on geodesy, and says he would revise sharply if a measured time dilation or drift surprised us.
responses.response: I take that seriously and I think it is the real scientific dispute, so I will not answer it by pointing to support counts. My answer is that the discovery in B049 is not about new physics beyond the standard framework but about a new regime that nature allows: many atoms interrogated at once with every perturbation controlled, shown by agreement between independent clocks at the 1e-18 level. The centimetre-level resolution of gravitational redshift between sites is a measured result, not a promise, even if the application to geodesy at scale is still to come, and null results on constants are themselves quantitative constraints that exist only because the clocks exist. I agree that B024 has a clearer discovery character, and I have moved it to the top of my alternatives for that reason. Where I still differ is that the theta-13 measurement is a parameter in a framework already honoured in 2015, and the credit among three near-simultaneous collaborations is harder to state, as you yourself acknowledge. If the committee decides that instruments count only after a surprise, then B024 is the better prize; I do not read the prize criteria that narrowly.

responses.point: Pearce proposes B049 plus a second part, B047 for Halzen alone, and holds the second part as droppable if his decisive role cannot be documented.
responses.response: I do not support B047 as a second part on the present material, and I would say so even though I find the diffuse flux measurement convincing. The chair has asked whether anyone can document a defensible one-to-three-person attribution, and I cannot: the supplied credit is a single name for a detector built and analysed by hundreds, with the AMANDA lineage in the background, and the source identifications rest on a single instrument. A two-part prize is also a structural choice, not just an add-on. I do not see a scientific reason to pair a metrology prize with neutrino astronomy unless both parts are individually secure, and I would rather award one secure part than two where one is contestable. If the committee finds a defensible set of names for IceCube, I would revisit it as a separate achievement, and I would then be glad to see it in a future cycle. I agree with you that the citation should name the concept and its realization, and I have written mine that way.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B048 as a compound theory-plus-experiment citation and argues it opened a new class of states of matter, which he weights above a parameter measurement or a precision result.
responses.response: I accept that B048 is the most mature of the condensed-matter candidates and I put it in my alternatives for that reason. The argument that the Z2 state is a distinct symmetry class from the 2016 prize is persuasive to me. My difficulty remains the credit: as Danielsson and Mehlig both note, the HgTe prediction came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the experiment that tested it is only decisive for existence, as you say, since the edge quantization is imperfect and I cannot judge from the exchange how well it has been reproduced outside Molenkamp's group. For a measurement-driven reader, that last point matters: the clock numbers are reproduced across several national laboratories and compared between them, while the HgTe edge result rests mainly on one group. If the committee is looking for a fallback with a clean discovery character, B048 and B024 are the two I would consider.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as discovery-class and distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or treats it as instrument performance, until a measured departure appears.

Whether a two-name credit for Katori and Ye is the right attribution, or whether the invention and realization belong to Katori alone with Ye's work as follow-on; I rely on recollection of the priority record and have not verified primary papers.
Whether other lattice-clock contributors (Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Lisdat, Ludlow and others) are adequately explained as outside the prize by a citation limited to the concept and its realization.
Whether the fallback, if B049 does not carry, should be B024 or B048, given their own credit disputes (Double Chooz and accelerator results; Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang).
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I did my PhD in Lund with a stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is a 2005 laureate in the frequency-comb lineage next to Ye's group at JILA; this is a distant mentoring connection, I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and I do not request recusal on B049. My research on rare-earth quantum memories is relevant to B001 and B044 and not to my configuration. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers (Johansson), relevant only to B038, which is not in my configuration. I have no tie to B024 or B048.
